name: PT Samator Indo Gas Tbk

frontmatter.title: Samator Indo Gas: a gas utility wearing a momentum premium
frontmatter.summary: AGII trades at Rp3,380 against our value today of 576.7 — 5.9 times it — after a run that twice drew a suspension and a company denial [S5][S6][S7]. The business is better than the data pack shows: depreciation was understated threefold, FY2025 EBITDA was IDR841.1bn and the nine-month margin is rising [S4][S2]. We rate SELL with a Rp2,148 target.
thesis: Our primary DCF gives Rp863 a share; the weighted blend is Rp623, the probability-weighted, liquidity-adjusted twelve-month fundamental value is Rp632, and the price is 5.9 times our value today of 576.7 [S0][S8].

The two multiple cross-checks sit far below the DCF (-61.8% and -82.3%); the engine applies the peer median to trailing FY2025A EBITDA of IDR831.6bn and trailing net profit of IDR58.4bn, so the divergence is partly a basis effect, and on the name's own four-year mean the price is at, not above, its historical EV/EBITDA [S0].

Operating momentum is real: nine-month revenue grew 7.5 per cent, the EBITDA margin reached 29.9 per cent and net profit rose to IDR114.3bn on cost of goods sold that grew slower than sales, while operating cash flow of IDR347.2bn less nine-month capex left the business cash-generative [S2][S3].
The equity is a thin lever: net debt to EBITDA is 3.5x, interest cover is thin, the rupiah bond coupons run into double digits and the payout is already IDR35.0bn a year [S2][S4][S8].

The premium is a flow story, not an earnings story: public holders own 7.6 per cent, HSC-designated shares left the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 [S10], the free float must step up 5.2% to 12.5% within 4.8 months, and that block is worth more than a year of the stock's turnover — supply that argues for faster convergence, not slower [S8][S9][S10].
What would change our mind is a strategic exit for the CVC stake or a free-float sell-down at a premium that puts real paper into the market without killing the price [S8].

catalysts.event: HSC-designated shares, AGII among them, leave the IHSG calculation — the passive bid for the stock is withdrawn
Maturity of the 2021 bond tranches — the refinancing test ahead of the float deadline
Free-float step-up deadline: the public float has to reach the next regulatory tier, by controller sell-down or new shares
FY2026 audited accounts and annual report — the first full year that carries the restated depreciation base and the 2025 capacity additions
MSCI consultation feedback closes on Indonesia's proposed standalone status (market-wide, not company-specific)
MSCI decision on Indonesia's index classification, the single largest external swing factor for a name held by so few hands

blocks.text: **The call.** SELL, target Rp2,148, against a close of Rp3,380: an expected return of -35.7% including the next twelve months of dividend at Rp26. This is not a call that Samator Indo Gas is a bad business. It is a call about what the market is paying for it. At the current price the shares change hands at 5.9 times our value today of 576.7 — the probability-weighted fundamental value for the year ahead after the liquidity discount, not the twelve-month fundamental value itself, which is Rp632 — and the house konglo lens keeps most of that gap in the base case, closing 40% of the logarithmic premium over twelve months [S0][S8].

**What the business is worth.** The primary method is a ten-year FCFF DCF at a WACC of 11.9%, which produces Rp863 a share and an enterprise value of IDR5,999.2bn, with the terminal value at 45.7% of the total. The two multiple cross-checks — Rp329 at 5.2 times EV/EBITDA and Rp153 at 8.0 times P/E — sit -61.8% and -82.3% below it, a divergence we take apart in section four rather than smooth away [S0].

**How the target is built.** The weighted blend of the three methods is Rp623 a share today. Rolling that forward at the cost of equity and deducting the next twelve months of dividend gives Rp682; probability-weighting our own operating scenarios gives Rp702; cutting 10% for a float this thin gives the fundamental value of Rp632; and applying the konglo premium-kept factor gives Rp2,148. Every step is visible in section four, which matters because a reviewer who sees only the first and last numbers will think one of them is a mistake.

**Why the price is where it is.** The shares closed at 1,560.0 on 6 October 2025, up roughly a quarter in a single session, and at 1,950.0 two sessions later after the exchange lifted a first suspension and the stock immediately ran again [S6][S5]. A second suspension followed in March 2026 [S7]. Through it all the company said publicly that it had no part in the move and that all material information had been disclosed [S6]. The twelve-month range runs from 1,130.0 to 3,740.0 against a last price of Rp3,380, and the public holds 7.2% of the shares [S0][S8]. That is a supply and attention story, and it is the part of the valuation that carries the most uncertainty.

**The three things that move the value.** First, whether the plants commissioned in 2025 ramp at the pace management targets, because volume is the only durable driver of a business whose prices are indexed [S8]. Second, the discount rate: the sensitivity table shows a hundred-basis-point move in the WACC is worth roughly a quarter of the DCF value, and even its most favourable cell does not reach the price — so the gap between our number and the tape cannot be closed by a lower cost of capital alone [S0]. Third, the flow: an HSC name now outside the IHSG calculation, with a free-float step due in 4.8 months and a block to place worth more than a year of turnover, faces a supply calendar that works against the premium, while a strategic exit for the CVC-managed stake is the one route by which it survives our twelve-month horizon [S8][S9][S10].

**What it is.** PT Samator Indo Gas Tbk is the largest producer and distributor of industrial gases in Indonesia, operating 60 production plants and a filling-station network that reaches thirty of the country's thirty-eight provinces, with around 1,687 employees [S8]. The company listed in 2016 and renamed itself from Aneka Gas Industri to Samator Indo Gas at the end of 2022 as part of a group identity consolidation, with the controlling family's stake unchanged through the change [S8]. Its origin explains the shape of it: the business began as the Indonesian arm of Messer, which sold its holding to PT Tira Austenite and the Harsono family in 2003, and the family has controlled the company ever since [S8].

**Products.** The portfolio splits into air gases — oxygen, nitrogen and argon separated from the atmosphere in air-separation units — and non-air gases, which cover hydrogen, carbon dioxide, acetylene, helium, specialty gases and calibration mixtures [S6][S8]. Around the molecules sits a service business: the design and installation of distribution systems, cylinder supply under rental arrangements, on-site plants built at a customer's fence line, and maintenance of the installed base [S6][S8]. The company's own description of the split and of the two product families is in the public expose it made when the exchange first questioned the share price [S6].

**Where it is strong.** Medical gases are the franchise: the company reports a share of roughly 75 per cent and above, held through hospital contracts and the oxygen supply relationships built during the pandemic [S8]. Cylinder and bulk industrial gases carry a share of about 40 per cent, which makes AGII the incumbent in a market where the alternative is a regional competitor with one plant and no national distribution [S8]. Volume was 729 thousand tonnes in 2025 against a company target of 838 thousand tonnes for 2026, a target that would require the new capacity to run at design rates [S8]. The unit deserves a note: the integrated report's production table states the same series in million cubic metres while its target table labels it in million tonnes, and we carry the tonnage label the target table uses rather than applying a density conversion the company does not disclose [S8].

**How it earns.** The bulk of revenue is contract-based rather than spot. On-site plants are written on take-or-pay minimum volumes, and the company renewed long-term contracts with foreign and domestic direct-investment customers through 2026, which is what gives the revenue line its low beta to industrial production [S2]. The retail cylinder business is the opposite: many small customers, annual repricing, and a competitive fringe that limits how far a price increase can run [S8]. Demand comes from healthcare, manufacturing, metal processing and electronics, and the company is actively pushing oxyfuel burners into glass and ceramics producers that cannot get enough natural gas [S2].

**Cost structure.** Cost of goods sold is dominated by manufacturing overhead at IDR1,102.0bn, or about two thirds of the total, with finished-goods trading, raw materials, direct labour and installation making up the rest [S4]. That mix matters for the model: electricity, plant labour and plant depreciation sit in overhead, and Indonesian electricity tariffs are administratively set off a coal benchmark rather than an oil one, so the Brent link that the sector card imposes on a CHEMICALS name is narrow here — we set the exposed share of cost of goods sold at twelve per cent and the pass-through at eighty-five per cent [S4][S2].

An industrial gas business is local before it is global. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap per tonne and expensive to move, so the economics are decided by how close the air-separation unit sits to the customer's fence and how dense the cylinder distribution is around it. That is why national networks matter more than technology: the separation process is old, well understood and licensed to anyone who will pay for it. The scarce assets are permits, land near industrial estates, a fleet of cylinders already sitting on customers' sites, and the patience to build a plant before the contract is signed. The same physics explains why large customers eventually insource: a steel mill or a refinery that consumes enough gas will build its own unit and buy only the marginal tonne.

**Group and control.** PT Samator holds 35.2 per cent, PT Aneka Mega Energi — another Harsono-family vehicle — holds 15.0 per cent, Matrix Company Limited, managed by CVC Capital Partners, holds 32.2 per cent after a March 2023 placement, PT Saratoga Investama Sedaya holds 10.0 per cent, and the public holds 7.58 per cent in stakes each below five per cent [S8]. Control sits with the family through the first two holders; CVC is a financial minority with governance rights and, eventually, an exit to think about [S8].

**Size and growth.** The company does not publish a market size, and we do not invent one. What it does publish is its own growth model: management targets revenue growth of one and a half to two times GDP, against a working assumption of GDP growth in the low fives, and it repeated that ambition in the 2026 plan [S8]. The house macro deck has real GDP growth in the low fives for FY2027E and inflation near the top of the central bank's band, which is consistent with the company's framework. On that arithmetic the addressable pool grows at a high single-digit rate in nominal terms when industrial production is expanding, and the company's own delivery has been far below it — revenue compounded at a low single-digit rate over FY2023 to FY2025 [S8][S3].

**What drives demand.** Four end markets matter. Healthcare takes medical oxygen and nitrous oxide under hospital contracts and is the most defensible; manufacturing and metal processing take bulk oxygen for furnaces, cutting and welding; electronics and food take nitrogen for inerting and freezing; and construction and infrastructure take smaller volumes through the retail cylinder channel [S2][S8]. The 2026 story is that glass and ceramics producers, short of natural gas, are converting burners to oxyfuel, which raises oxygen intensity per unit of output — a genuine share-of-wallet gain for whoever holds the on-site contract [S2].

**Competitive structure.** AGII is the scale incumbent: the largest producer, the widest plant network and the only national cylinder distribution of any size [S8]. The competitive fringe is regional and fragmented, strongest in retail nitrogen and oxygen where the switching cost is a cylinder deposit, and weakest in on-site supply where the capital requirement and the take-or-pay contract lock the relationship for a decade [S8]. New entrants face three barriers — permits and land near industrial estates, the capital cost of an air-separation unit before any revenue, and the last-mile fleet — none of which is insurmountable individually and all of which together explain why the share has been stable rather than growing [S8].

**Five forces, in one paragraph.** Supplier power is the binding constraint, not buyer power: electricity is administered and feedstock for hydrogen and carbon dioxide tracks energy, while customers are large but contracted on take-or-pay terms that protect volume [S2][S4]. Buyer power shows up in the retail channel as annual price negotiation, which is why our pass-through assumption is high but not complete [S8]. Substitutes are real at the margin: a customer that can get pipeline natural gas may not need an oxyfuel conversion, and a customer with enough scale may build its own plant [S2]. Rivalry is moderate and local; the national share has not moved [S8]. The net position is a narrow moat built on distribution density and contracts rather than on product differentiation.

**Regulation and policy.** Four regulatory threads touch the name. The first is market structure: the exchange classes AGII as a high-shareholding-concentration stock, in a list that ran to 82 names at the last release [S9]. The second is index treatment: HSC-designated shares, AGII among them, left the IHSG calculation on Monday 2 November 2026, three days before this report, on top of the loss of LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 membership that HSC status already carried — the passive bid for the stock is now structurally smaller [S10][S9]. The third is the free-float regime, which sets a dated step-up the controlling holders have to meet either by selling down or by issuing shares [S8]. The fourth is pricing of inputs and outputs: electricity tariffs are administratively set and passed through with a lag, and medical gas supply is contracted against hospital budgets rather than market prices [S2][S4]. None of these is a licence risk; all of them are risks to the multiple.

**Commodity exposure.** The sector card prices AGII off Brent because it files as a chemical. We keep the link for discipline but size it honestly: the cost of goods sold note shows manufacturing overhead at two thirds of the total, and that block carries electricity and plant depreciation rather than hydrocarbons, so the Brent-sensitive slice is diesel for distribution, LPG and gas feedstock for hydrogen and carbon dioxide, and freight [S4][F32]. The model therefore exposes twelve per cent of cost of goods sold to Brent with eighty-five per cent pass-through, leaving roughly two per cent of cost exposed on a net basis [S4][S2].

**FY2025, restated.** Revenue was IDR3,008.8bn, gross profit IDR1,381.0bn and operating profit IDR401.0bn [S4]. The line that matters is depreciation: the audited note charges IDR430.5bn to profit or loss, of which the great majority sits inside cost of goods sold, while the data pack carries only the selling and administrative blocks and reports a fraction of it [S4][F7][S0]. On the correct figure, FY2025 EBITDA is IDR831.6bn — a margin of 27.6% — against the IDR841.1bn the company itself reported in its integrated report, the small difference being licence amortisation and other add-backs that we leave out of the model [S8][S4]. The pack's margin of just over one fifth was an artefact of the missing depreciation line, not a business fact.

**The nine months to September 2026.** Revenue reached IDR2,376.6bn, up 7.5 per cent, with cost of goods sold growing at a little over half the pace of revenue, so gross margin widened to 47.6 per cent from the prior-year comparative [S2][S3]. EBITDA was IDR709.4bn against IDR640.8bn a year earlier, a margin of 29.9 per cent, of which IDR46.9bn of net profit came in the third quarter alone, the strongest quarter of the year [S2]. Net profit for the nine months was IDR114.3bn, up by nearly four fifths, helped by lower net finance expense as gross debt came down and by higher interest income on cash [S2]. Operating expense grew faster than revenue, which the company attributes to distribution activity; the ratio to sales is nonetheless stable at about a third [S2][S3].

**The cost story.** The margin improvement is operating, not accounting. Management reports efficiency in plant cost, specifically electricity and labour per unit, and the arithmetic supports it: with revenue growing faster than cost of goods sold, the incremental gross margin is above the average [S2]. That is the good news and it is why our FY2026 gross margin assumption of forty-seven and a half per cent holds the nine-month actual rather than reverting to the FY2025 figure of forty-six per cent [S8][S3]. The company's own 2026 plan is more ambitious — a revenue target of IDR3,318.1bn and a gross-profit target of IDR1,866.4bn, the second implying a fifty-six per cent gross margin — and we do not use it: 2025 revenue came in at 92.1 per cent of the plan, and the margin target is far above anything the company has delivered, so the plan is a stretch target rather than a forecast [S8][F18][F19][F31].

**Cash flow and capital intensity.** The accounts are more cash-generative than the FCFF line implies. Operating cash flow was IDR451.4bn in FY2025 and IDR347.2bn in the nine months to September 2026 against IDR2,376.6bn of nine-month revenue; after capex of IDR427.3bn in FY2025 the group still funded a working-capital build and its dividend from operations, and the nine months ran well ahead of that pace, so the DCF's FY2026E free cash flow of IDR402.2bn is consistent with what the accounts actually delivered [S3][S4][S8]. The investment cycle peaked: committed capital expenditure fell to IDR143.0bn at end-2025 from a multiple of that a year earlier as the new plants were completed [S8]. Our forecast then steps cash capital expenditure back up from eight per cent of revenue to the fourteen per cent depreciation charge by the terminal year, as growth spending resumes and the asset base has to be replaced, which is why free cash flow rises more slowly than EBITDA over the forecast [S8][S4].

**Working capital and the balance sheet.** Operating working capital was IDR916.1bn at end-2025 and we model it at about a third of revenue, above the historical ratio, because trade receivables and inventories both built through 2026 [S3][S4]. The receivables build deserves the flag the earnings-quality card sets: trade receivables were IDR761.0bn at 30 September 2026 against IDR677.0bn at 31 December 2025, growth well ahead of revenue growth of 7.5 per cent, and the third-party balance did the building while related-party receivables fell — so this is a collection and mix question on third-party customers rather than a related-party channel stuffing, and we watch the ageing and the cash-conversion trend rather than assume it reverses [S3][S4]. Gross debt was reduced in the nine months, part of it US-dollar denominated, and the company reports net debt to EBITDA of 3.5x against a higher figure a year earlier, with EBITDA covering interest about three times [S2][S3]. The rupiah bond and sukuk coupons run from about nine per cent to above eleven per cent, so the blended cash cost of debt we use in the P&L is a little under nine per cent, consistent with the FY2025 finance charge of IDR325.9bn on opening gross debt [S3][S4].

**Dividend and capital allocation.** The company paid IDR35.0bn to shareholders out of FY2025 profit, a payout of about three fifths of parent earnings and a dividend per share of Rp11 [S3][S8]. Our forecast holds that payout ratio rather than cutting to the statutory floor, because the last actual is the better guide to intent and because payout does not change the unlevered value [S3].

**Forecast.** We model revenue of IDR3,234.5bn for FY2026E — a mid single-digit increase on FY2025, built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter growing at the nine-month pace of 7.5 per cent, because no archived source gives a quarterly revenue series and the company's own target would require an implausible fourth-quarter acceleration [S3][S8]. From FY2027E growth steps to nine per cent, the low end of management's GDP-linked model and the first full year of the 2025 plants, then decays to IDR5,861.0bn of revenue by FY2035E as the capacity ramp matures [S8]. EBITDA reaches IDR941.6bn in FY2026E at a 29.1% margin and net profit IDR133.2bn, taking earnings per share to Rp43 from Rp19 [S3]. Leverage falls steadily, to 2.5 by FY2028E and 1.8 by FY2030E, on flat gross debt and rising cash rather than on any assumption of asset sales [S4][S3].

**Earnings-quality flags.** Five items deserve the red team's attention. First, the depreciation omission in the pack is the single largest data error we found and it changes every margin in the historical series [S4][S0]. Second, depreciation at fourteen per cent of revenue sits above cash capital expenditure for most of the forecast, and that gap is the largest valuation question in the model. In the near term it is genuine: cylinder, tank and vehicle renewal is lease-financed, lease principal of IDR106.0bn was repaid in the nine months against IDR60.6bn of new leases, and the lease liability sits inside the gross debt we deduct in the equity bridge, so adding the principal to capex as well would charge the same obligation twice [S3][S4]. But the gap cannot persist into a perpetuity: left alone it leaves roughly three and a half points of revenue a year of depreciation unfunded, and capitalising that residual in the terminal value would flatter the valuation. We therefore lift cash capex to the depreciation rate by FY2035E, so terminal-year capital expenditure is IDR826.4bn against D&A of IDR826.4bn, and the DCF is Rp863 rather than the materially higher figure the unfunded path produced [S3][S4][S8]. Third, related-party sales were IDR149.7bn in FY2025 and IDR97.8bn in the nine months of 2026, around a twentieth and a twenty-fifth of revenue, and a meaningful slice of trade receivables is due from related parties [S4][S3]. Fourth, the effective tax rate is unstable — thirty per cent in FY2025 on a small pre-tax base and under eighteen per cent in the nine months — so we forecast the statutory twenty-two per cent and let the reader see the sensitivity [S4][S3]. Fifth, part of the bank debt is in US dollars and the rupiah weakened against the dollar through 2026, which inflates both the debt stock and the finance charge in rupiah terms without changing the operating business [S3].

Two accounting habits make industrial gas earnings harder to read than they look. Depreciation is spread across cost of goods sold and both operating expense lines, so any data source that reads only the income-statement subtotals will miss most of it and report a margin that is too high. And because cylinders and tanks are long-lived assets that sit on customers' sites, a company can either buy them and depreciate them or lease them and pay a financing charge; the two routes give the same economics but very different EBITDA, capital expenditure and debt. Neither habit is a red flag on its own. Both are the reason a first pass at this name produces a margin that does not reconcile with the audited accounts.

**Why this method set.** The cash flows are contracted, indexed and long-lived, and the asset base is capital-intensive and expanding, which is the case for a discounted cash flow as the primary method. Multiples are a cross-check on what the market is paying for the same stream, and because the sector card sets the weights at sixty per cent DCF, twenty-five per cent EV/EBITDA and fifteen per cent P/E, we run all three and show the divergence rather than hiding it [S0].
**Cost of capital.**

The build is the house one, and the full bridge is: a risk-free rate of 7.4% on the ten-year, less the 1.6% Indonesian default spread the macro deck deducts from the domestic risk-free rate before it is used as the equity base, plus 1.16 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 13.6%. The unlevered beta of 0.90 is the industry default, relevered at the company's debt-to-equity of 0.37 and a tax rate of twenty-two per cent. Debt enters at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, which is the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread of 0.0 — a marginal cost, deliberately higher than the company's actual cash cost of debt used in the P&L path, because the existing book is fixed-coupon paper issued before the 2026 rise and would be refinanced dearer. At a debt weight of 27.2% that gives a WACC of 11.9%. The cost of equity is the number that decides this valuation, and at a rate in the low teens no plausible operating forecast reaches the current price [S0].
**The DCF.**

Explicit free cash flow rises from IDR402.2bn in FY2026E to IDR584.2bn in FY2035E, terminal growth is four per cent, and the terminal value is 45.7% of the enterprise value of IDR5,999.2bn. After gross debt at 30 September of IDR3,877.5bn less cash of IDR612.4bn — a net debt of about three and a quarter trillion rupiah — minorities of IDR88.5bn and no associate or investment offset, the equity value is Rp863 a share [S3][S0]. The terminal share is now under half, after the reinvestment rate converges on the depreciation charge, which is low enough that the conclusion does not rest on the terminal assumption alone. That convergence matters: an earlier draft held capex below D&A through the forecast, left about three and a half points of revenue a year of depreciation unfunded, and capitalised the residual in the terminal value; lifting capex to the depreciation rate by FY2035E takes the DCF from a level near a third higher to Rp863 and the target to Rp2,148, and the move is value-reducing, so the SELL widens rather than narrows [S0][S4].
**The multiple cross-checks, and why they disagree.**

The EV/EBITDA leg applies the peer median of 5.2 times to the engine's trailing metric, FY2025A EBITDA of IDR831.6bn, and lands at Rp329, -61.8% below the DCF; the P/E leg applies 8.0 times trailing FY2025A net profit of IDR58.4bn and lands at Rp153, -82.3% below [S0]. Both are trailing legs, not forward ones, and on our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR941.6bn and net profit of IDR133.2bn the same multiples would give materially higher values — the divergence is a basis effect as well as a comparator effect, and we say so rather than let the headline percentages stand alone. The deeper reason is the comparator set: the CHEMICALS peer group in this market is a commodity petrochemical complex with a different margin structure, a different cycle and a different leverage profile, and its median multiple of under six times EBITDA is not a description of a business that earns thirty per cent margins on contracted gas volumes [S0][S2]. We keep the weights because the method card sets them and because a cross-check that only confirms the primary is not a cross-check, but we do not let a mis-specified peer set drive the rating: the DCF is the anchor, the multiples are a warning about how the market prices the industry rather than about this company.

**The own-history cross-check.** The model also carries the name's own four-year multiple history, and it is the most uncomfortable number in this report: the mean EV/EBITDA over that period is the same 14.5x the shares trade on today, and the mean P/E is of the same order as the FY2027E multiple of 59.0x [S0]. On its own history the stock is not an outlier — it is at its norm. We do not take that as validation, because the history it averages is the very re-rating that took the shares from a mid-single-digit EV/EBITDA to today's level, so the mean embeds the premium rather than testing it; but it does mean the honest statement is that the market has consistently paid this multiple for this asset, and our case rests on the DCF showing that the cash flows do not support it, not on the market being irrational [S0][S8].

**What the market is paying.** At Rp3,380 the shares trade on 14.5x forward EV/EBITDA and 77.8x forward earnings, and on 2.7x book [S0]. Those are the multiples of a global industrial gas major, applied to a company with three and a half turns of leverage, a seven per cent free float and a country risk premium in its cost of capital [S2][S8]. The reverse DCF makes the same point from the other side: held to our WACC and our margins, the price cannot be reached by any revenue-growth rate the solver will accept, so the market is not paying for a faster ramp — it is paying a price our operating assumptions cannot produce at any discount rate in the table [S0]. That is why we do not frame this as a rate call: the sensitivity grid shows the most favourable cell — a full point off the WACC and a point on terminal growth — still below the price, so a lower cost of capital narrows the gap without closing it, and only a re-rating on flow or a strategic bid does that [S0].

**Target construction, step by step.** The weighted blend is Rp623 today. Rolling forward one year at the cost of equity of 13.6% and deducting the next twelve months of dividend of Rp26 gives Rp682. Probability-weighting the bear, base and bull model runs gives Rp702. Cutting 10% for illiquidity — three-month turnover is about a billion rupiah a day, which puts the name in the widest band in the house table — gives Rp632 [S0]. That is the fundamental twelve-month value, and it is what a holder should expect to receive if the premium disappeared entirely.

**The konglo lens, and why the target is above the fundamental value.** AGII qualifies as a konglo name: a controlling family, a large financial minority, a free float of 7.2%, and a place on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S8][S9]. The house lens therefore does not assume the premium disappears — it assumes a fraction of it closes. The price sits 5.9 times our value today, a logarithmic gap of 1.8. The regime run applies closures of 80%, 40% and -5% of that gap in the bear, base and bull cases, weighted a quarter, a half and a quarter, giving Rp900, Rp1,825 and Rp4,044. The deck base closure of 30% is lifted to 40% by the two name-specific flags — HSC membership and the free-float deadline inside the window — each adding five points of closure, because the code adds the adjustment to the share of the gap that closes, not to the premium that is kept: the flags make the premium close faster [S8][S9].

**The float arithmetic.** That direction matters because the supply calendar is explicit. The free float of 7.2% has to reach 12.5% by 4.8 months out — a 5.2% step on 3,066.7m shares, which at Rp3,380 is a block worth more than a year of the stock's three-month average daily turnover of about a billion rupiah [S0][S8]. Whether it is sold down by the controllers or issued, that is supply the market has to absorb inside the window, and it argues for more closing, not less: the base case still keeps the premium at more than twice our value today after the adjustment [S9][S8]. A placement to long-only holders at a premium is the one mechanism that absorbs the block without the price giving way, which is why the bull regime — where the gap re-expands — is the honest description of the upside case [S8].
**Sensitivity.**

The two variables that matter are the terminal growth rate and the WACC, and the grid is the answer to the rate-call question: a hundred basis points on the discount rate moves the DCF value by roughly a quarter, and even the most favourable cell in the table — a full point lower on the WACC and a point higher on terminal growth — remains below the price [S0]. So the gap is not a rate call, and we do not make that claim. The forecast itself is not especially aggressive — nine per cent revenue growth against a compound three and a half per cent actually delivered over the last three years, and a margin held at the nine-month actual [S8][S3]. If anything the operating assumptions are generous; the target is low because the price is high.

**The risk that dominates.** The premium is the risk. Our bear case does not require the business to deteriorate — it requires the multiple to normalise toward the DCF, which is what happens to concentrated-ownership names when the flow that lifted them reverses. The bear value is Rp415 against Rp682 in the base and Rp1,029 in the bull, on probabilities of a quarter, a half and a quarter respectively [S0]. Note that the operating bull case, which raises growth by three points and margin by a point and a half, still produces a value below today's price: the only case in this report that reaches the price is the konglo regime bull at Rp4,044, where the premium re-expands because a strategic buyer or an index re-inclusion resets what the float is worth [S8][S10]. That is the honest shape of the upside, and we state it rather than capping the bull.

**The supply calendar.** Three dates sit inside the next twelve months and all of them bear on the premium. The HSC names left the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026, which removes the passive bid without removing a single share [S10][S9]. The free float has to reach 12.5% by the end of March 2027, a 5.2% step that is a block worth more than a year of the stock's average daily turnover at today's price — supply the tape has to absorb, whether it arrives as a sell-down or as new shares [S8][S0]. And the 22 December 2026 bond maturity and the rupiah current maturities fall in the same window, so the company and the controllers are both in the market for capital at once [S3].

**Upside risks to a SELL.** Three are credible. A strategic buyer for the CVC-managed stake at a price above the market would validate the premium and could force a tender [S8]. A free-float sell-down that places a large block with long-only holders would fix the liquidity discount and could narrow the gap we apply — the float has to rise to the next regulatory tier by the deadline, and how it is done decides whether the price holds [S8]. And the operating ramp could beat us: the 2025 plants were commissioned into a market where glass and ceramics are converting to oxyfuel, and a fast ramp would lift the DCF by more than our sensitivity table shows [S2][S8].

**Downside risks beyond the multiple.** Leverage is the first: net debt to EBITDA of 3.5x with interest cover of about three times leaves little room if margins compress, and the bond coupons of nine to eleven per cent mean refinancing is expensive [S2][S3]. Electricity tariffs are the second: they are administered, they are the largest single cost in manufacturing overhead, and a tariff increase that cannot be passed through in the same year hits gross margin directly [S4]. Customer concentration and receivables are the third: related-party sales are a twentieth of revenue and related-party receivables are a visible slice of the balance sheet, so a related-party stress would show up as a cash problem before it showed up as an earnings problem [S4][S3]. Currency is the fourth: part of the debt is dollar-denominated and the rupiah has weakened, which raises the rupiah debt stock and the finance charge without any operating change [S3].
**Scenario analysis and the konglo regimes.**

The operating scenarios shock revenue growth by three points and gross margin by a point and a half in each direction, and carry the probabilities in the frontmatter. The konglo regimes are a separate axis and are not additive to them: the lens applied to the probability-weighted fundamental value produces Rp900, Rp1,825 and Rp4,044 for gap closures of eighty, forty and minus five per cent, and the weighted result is the Rp2,148 target [S8][S9]. Reading the two together, the base case is a business that compounds modestly while the multiple gives back two fifths of its premium; the bear is both at once, and that is the case worth sizing against.

**Signposts that change the view.** We would move to a hold on a credible strategic transaction for the minority stake, on a float increase that brings the public holding above the regulatory step without a discount, or on a first half of 2027 in which volume growth exceeds the target while the gross margin holds above the nine-month level [S8][S2]. We would move to a deeper sell on a failure to meet the float deadline, on a refinancing at a materially higher coupon, or on the exchange adding the name to an enforcement list rather than a disclosure list [S9][S3].

**Ownership and control.** The Harsono family controls the company through PT Samator at 35.2 per cent and PT Aneka Mega Energi at 15.0 per cent; Matrix Company Limited, managed by CVC, holds 32.2 per cent; Saratoga holds 10.0 per cent; and the public holds 7.58 per cent, in each case below five per cent individually [S8]. The president director and his deputy both carry the controlling family's surname, and the board has independent commissioners as required, but the practical governance question for a minority holder is not board composition — it is what the two largest holders do with their stakes [S2][S6].

**Related-party dealings.** Sales to related parties were IDR149.7bn in FY2025 and IDR97.8bn in the first nine months of 2026, and the receivables note shows related-party balances among trade receivables [S4][S3]. The amounts are disclosed and priced in the ordinary course, and the nine-month ratio is lower than the full-year ratio, which is the right direction. It nonetheless means a fifth of the receivables book depends on entities the controlling family also controls, and that is a governance exposure rather than an accounting one.

**Market-conduct record.** The shares were suspended twice for cumulative price increases — October 2025 and March 2026 — and the company responded with a public expose in which it stated that it had no involvement in the price movement and that all material information had been disclosed [S5][S6][S7]. We found no enforcement action, no unusual-market-activity finding against the company, and no restatement in the sources we archived [S9][S4]. What we did find is a name that remains on the high-shareholding-concentration list at the latest release, with a public float of 7.2% that has to reach 12.5% by the deadline in the frontmatter, against the statutory minimum float [S9][S8]. The two float numbers in this report are different dates on the same shrinking base: the integrated report's 7.58 per cent is the 31 December 2025 register, the konglo registry's 7.2% is the current figure we and the engine use, and the difference is disclosure-driven rather than a change in the register [S8][S0]. HSC is a disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing; it is nonetheless the single best predictor of which names get the flow and which lose it in this market regime — and since 2 November 2026 it has cost the name its IHSG weight as well [S9][S10].

**Audit and reporting.** The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion from KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, an Ernst and Young member firm, on an Indonesian GAAP basis [S4]. Reporting quality is adequate: the depreciation note, the cost-of-goods-sold mix and the related-party note are all disclosed at the level needed to rebuild the economics, which is more than can be said for many names in this market. The one date question in the accounts is now closed. The equity bridge runs on a single date, 30 September 2026: gross debt of IDR3,877.5bn from the financing-activities note — bank loans, bonds and sukuk, leases and other borrowings together — less the 30 September cash balance [S3][F52][F22]. That replaces an earlier mix of 30 June debt with 30 September cash and, with the DCF time zero now discounting FY2026E from the same 30 September date, the two halves of the valuation finally sit on one balance sheet; the restatement cuts net debt by about forty-nine billion rupiah, adding roughly sixteen rupiah a share, or well under one per cent of the target [S3][S0].

**ESG exposures.** The environmental profile is an electricity story: air separation is power-intensive, so the scope-two footprint follows the grid, and the company's decarbonisation levers are efficiency and renewable power contracts rather than process change [S8]. Safety is the material social issue — high-pressure gases, cryogenic liquids and medical oxygen — and the company reports the certifications and procedures expected of a supplier to hospitals [S8]. Governance is where the score is weakest, for the reasons above: control concentration, a thin float and a related-party channel. None of these is a reason to own or not own the stock at this price; all of them are part of why the discount rate we apply is what it is.

**Dated catalysts.** The HSC exclusion took effect on 2 November 2026, three days before this report: the shares lost their IHSG weight, and section four's base case carries the consequence [S10][S9]. The FY2026 audited accounts at the end of April 2027 are the first full-year test of the restated depreciation base, the 2025 capacity additions and the dividend policy [S3][S8]. The free-float step-up deadline at the end of March 2027 is the corporate-action catalyst: how the controlling holders close the gap decides both the supply of stock and the credibility of the premium [S8]. The 22 December 2026 maturity of the 2021 bond tranches sits inside the same window and tests the refinancing market before the float deadline does [S3]. The MSCI consultation on Indonesia's classification closes for feedback at the end of April 2027 and a decision is due by the end of June 2027; for a name this thinly held, an index decision is a bigger swing factor than any quarter's volume [S9].

**What we monitor between updates.** Volume against the company's own target of 838 thousand tonnes, reported annually in the integrated report rather than in the interim accounts [S8]. The gross margin, because it is the cleanest read on whether the electricity and labour efficiency is durable [S2]. Net debt to EBITDA and the interest cover, because the equity is a thin lever on a business with expensive rupiah debt [S2]. The free float and the composition of the register, because they determine the discount we apply and the speed at which the premium closes [S8][S9]. And the exchange's concentration list and any unusual-market-activity notices, because in this regime they move the price more than the fundamentals do [S9].

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +7.5% is built from the nine-month actual of Rp2,376.6bn (F9) plus a fourth quarter growing at the nine-month pace of +7.5% (F42) on Q4 2025, which is the only growth rate the archived sources carry: S3 has no quarterly revenue columns, and the Q3 profit and EBITDA prints (F30, S2) do not give Q3 revenue. The company's own 2026 target of Rp3,318.1bn (+10.3%) needs a Q4 acceleration to double digits and is not the most likely path [S3, S8, S2, F42]. From FY2027E we use +9%, the low end of management's stated 1.5-2.0x GDP growth model (GDP 5.1-5.3%) and the first full year of the three plants commissioned in 2025, then +8%, +7.5% and +7.0% as the capacity ramp matures, against a compound 3.5% actually delivered over FY2023-FY2025 [S8, S3, S0]. Long-run 6.0% is below nominal GDP because a 40%-share incumbent grows with the industrial gas pool, not faster than it [S8, F14].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 47.5% is the nine-month 2026 actual of 47.6%, held flat rather than carried back to the FY2025 45.90%: the last actual is the anchor, and the improvement is operating (cost of goods sold grew 4.3% against revenue of 7.5%, with electricity and direct labour per unit falling), not a one-off gain [S2, S3, S8]. The company's 2026 target of Rp1,866.4bn of gross profit implies 56.2% and is treated as a stretch target, not a forecast; 2025 delivery was only 75.7% of the gross-profit target [S8, F19, F31]. No margin haircut is applied: the cost base is held at the last actual in real terms [S8].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a company disclosure: 12% of cost of goods sold is treated as Brent-exposed. The COGS note splits the Rp1,627.8bn into finished-goods trading 16%, raw materials 5%, direct labour 4%, manufacturing overhead 68% and installation 7%; the overhead carries PLN electricity and plant depreciation, and PLN tariffs are set administratively off coal, so the Brent-sensitive slice is diesel distribution, LPG/natural-gas feedstock and freight [S4, F32]. Any larger share would import a petrochemical cost structure the company does not have.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibration: 85% of an energy-cost move is recovered in selling prices, because industrial gas contracts are indexed and the company reprices cylinder and bulk gas annually; the residual 15% is the lag and the competitive constraint in retail nitrogen and oxygen, where the 40% market share still leaves regional competitors [S8, F14, S2]. The pair leaves a net 1.8% of COGS exposed to Brent, which is consistent with FY2025's 45.90% gross margin at an average Brent of US$68 and 9M2026's 47.6% at a higher Brent, once the cost efficiency the company reports is allowed for [S8, S2, S4].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 32.1% is the nine-month 2026 actual: selling Rp470.7bn plus general and administrative Rp289.0bn plus net other expense Rp3.9bn on revenue of Rp2,376.6bn, with depreciation left inside both blocks because that is where this LK presents it [S3]. FY2025 was 32.6%, so the ratio is stable and slightly improving on the digitalisation programme (auto-invoicing on 65% of invoices, e-Faktur on 93%) [S8, S4]. Held flat; no margin expansion is assumed from operating leverage beyond what the last actual shows [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 14.1% of revenue: total depreciation charged to profit or loss was Rp335.1bn in the nine months to September 2026 (COGS Rp211.4bn, selling Rp84.4bn, G&A Rp39.3bn), 14.1% of revenue, against Rp430.5bn or 14.3% in FY2025 [S3, S4, F7]. The data pack's 4.8% default is wrong by a factor of three because Yahoo reads only the selling and administrative depreciation and misses the Rp291.3bn inside cost of goods sold; the facts restate both fiscal years [S4, S0]. Licence amortisation of Rp8.0bn sits in G&A and is left out of this line, which understates EBITDA by about 0.3% of revenue [S3].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 8.0% for FY2026E: cash capital expenditure was Rp188.9bn in the nine months to September 2026 (Rp151.0bn of fixed assets plus Rp38.0bn of advances), 7.9% of revenue, and committed capex had fallen to Rp143bn at end-2025 from Rp490bn a year earlier as the three new plants were commissioned [S3, S8, F17]. The path then steps up as growth capex resumes for the specialty and mixed gas build-out and the 2025 plants are debottlenecked, and from FY2031E it converges on the D&A charge, reaching 14.1% of revenue by FY2035E and holding there. A perpetuity cannot reinvest less than it depreciates: the early gap is the growth phase, when the newly commissioned asset base is underutilised and cylinder renewal is lease-financed - lease principal of Rp106.0bn was repaid in the nine months against Rp60.6bn of new leases (F50, F51) and the lease liability sits inside gross debt, so that near-term renewal is already charged through net debt and the cost of debt - but by the terminal year the whole asset base, owned and leased, has to be replaced, so cash capex must match the 14.1% depreciation rate rather than the 10.8% earlier draft [S3, S4, S8].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 33.7% at 30 September 2026 on the engine's definition (current assets less cash, less current liabilities net of current debt): Rp2,068.5bn less Rp612.4bn cash, against Rp1,075.5bn of current liabilities of which Rp686.7bn is short-term debt, equals Rp1,067.3bn on annualised revenue [S3]. That is above FY2025's 30.5% because trade receivables rose to Rp760.9bn (including Rp152.9bn from related parties) and inventories to Rp512.1bn; we normalise to 33.0% from FY2027E as the receivable build reverses, not below the FY2025 ratio [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22% statutory. The FY2025 effective rate was 30.6% on a small pre-tax base because of non-deductible items, and the nine-month 2026 rate was 17.6%; the forward rate is the statutory 22% rather than either observed year, since neither is a structural rate [S4, S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.4%: nine-month 2026 finance expenses of Rp244.0bn annualise to Rp325.3bn against average gross debt of about Rp3.9trn [S3]. The bond and sukuk coupons run 9.15%-11.25% and bank facilities sit below that, so 8.4% is the blended cash cost; it also matches the FY2025 charge of Rp325.9bn on opening debt of Rp3,629.5bn [S4, S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: nine-month 2026 interest income of Rp16.3bn annualises to Rp21.8bn on cash of Rp612.4bn, but cash averaged higher through the year and FY2025 earned Rp18.1bn on average cash near Rp500bn, so 4.0% is the sustainable yield [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -Rp50bn: gross debt fell from Rp3,984.9bn at end-2025 to Rp3,877.5bn at 30 September 2026 (bank loans Rp2,937.9bn, bonds and sukuk Rp740.7bn, leases Rp196.9bn, financial institutions Rp2.1bn) and the company targets a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.06x against 1.20x, so the base repays modestly [S3, S8]. Thereafter no net new borrowing: free cash flow covers capex, interest and the dividend, and we do not credit further deleveraging because it would be a value assumption dressed as financing [S3, S8].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. The net other expense line (Rp3.9bn in the nine months, Rp10.4bn in FY2025) is management fees, tax expense and small asset-disposal gains; it is already inside the opex ratio and is not forecast as a separate recurring item [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: minorities took Rp4.04bn of nine-month 2026 profit of Rp114.3bn (3.5%) and Rp4.23bn of FY2025's Rp62.6bn (6.8%); the three minority vehicles are PT Samator Gas Industri, PT Ruci Gas and PT Krakatau Samator, whose combined share is stable [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 60% of parent earnings, the last actual: the Rp35.0bn paid in 2026 out of FY2025 profit of Rp58.4bn is Rp11.42 a share, against the statutory floor of 20% of operating profit and Rp8.56 a share a year earlier [S3, F28, S8]. We hold the last actual rather than cut to the floor; payout is a financing choice and does not change the unlevered value [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,066.66m shares issued and fully paid, unchanged since the 2023 placement; no buyback, rights issue or convertible is outstanding [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%, the house rupiah terminal rate: below long-run nominal GDP (real GDP 5.1-5.3% plus 3.3% CPI), which is the right bound for a mature industrial gas incumbent whose volumes grow with manufacturing output rather than faster than it [S8, kb macro deck].

challenges.challenge: The report is silent on the index event its own framework calls the biggest flow driver. The company news log carries a material item dated 2026-11-01: HSC-designated shares leave the IHSG calculation from Monday 2 November 2026 (investasi.kontan.co.id). The report instead says the name remains on the HSC list at the 26 Oct release [S9] and the post_bs_review states that the only market event is AGII continued presence on that list. The model own konglo adjustment says HSC names are out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes. A dated passive-flow deletion three days before the report date is omitted from sections 2, 5, 6 and 7.
challenges.answer: Fixed on substance. Registered S10 (liputan6, 1-2 Nov 2026) confirming that HSC-designated shares left the IHSG calculation on Monday 2 November 2026, and AGII is on that list [S9][S10]. Added the exclusion with the memberships lost (IHSG weight now, LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and MSCI treatment via HSC status) to section 2 regulation, section 6 market conduct, section 7 catalysts and the frontmatter catalyst table. Corrected the post_bs_review sentence that called continued HSC presence the only market event. The base-case compression in section 4 is now argued against the flow calendar, not just the deck default.

challenges.challenge: The 40% base-case closure of the log gap is the deck default with no name-specific support, and the report explanation of the two +5% flags is backwards. fund record adds adj_total (+0.10) to the CLOSING share, so compress 0.3/0.7/-0.15 becomes 0.4/0.8/-0.05: the flags make the premium close faster, not add five per cent to the retained premium, and the base is 47% of the way from bear to bull, not a quarter. The konglo card section 4 requires the float math for THIS name: the registry gives free float 7.25% against a 12.5% step by 2027-03-31, a 5.25pp gap of about 161m shares, Rp547bn at Rp3,400, roughly 520 days of the Rp1.05bn ADTV, inside 4.8 months. That supply calendar argues for more compression, not less, and the report never mentions it.
challenges.answer: The flag direction is corrected: the code adds adj_total to the CLOSING share, so deck 0.3/0.7/-0.15 becomes 0.4/0.8/-0.05 and the flags make the premium close faster, not add to the retained premium; the report now says exactly that and drops the wrong quarter-of-the-way claim (the base is 47% of the way from bear to bull). Float arithmetic added to sections 4 and 5: gap 5.25pp on 3,066.66m shares = 161m shares, Rp547bn at the Rp3,400 price, about 520 days of the Rp1.05bn ADTV, due 31 March 2027 inside 4.8 months [S8][S0][S9]. The 40% closure is the reviewed deck base of 30% plus two name-specific 5pt flags (HSC, ff deadline); the supply calendar argues for MORE compression, so the base is if anything generous to the premium, and we keep it rather than hand-edit a house deck that governs every konglo name.

challenges.challenge: The multiple cross-checks are described as forward but the engine applies them to trailing FY2025A metrics: ev_ebitda metric 831.552 (FY2025A EBITDA) and pe metric 58.379 (FY2025A NP), giving Rp492 and Rp159. On the FY2026E metrics the report says it uses, the legs are about Rp693 and Rp356, so the -60.0%/-87.1% divergence is overstated by roughly Rp200 a share on each leg. The report also ignores the own_history block in its own model: four-year mean EV/EBITDA 14.58x against 14.64x at the price, and P/E mean 53.9x, which says the market is at the name own historical multiple, not at a global-major anomaly.
challenges.answer: Basis corrected: the report now says the engine applies 5.907x to trailing FY2025A EBITDA of 831.552 and 8.346x to trailing FY2025A net profit of 58.379, and prints the forward FY2026E EBITDA and net profit beside them so the reader can see the basis effect. Section 4 gains an own-history cross-check: the four-year mean EV/EBITDA of 14.58x is the same as the 14.55x the shares trade on today and the mean P/E of 53.9x is the same order as the FY2027E 60.2x - the market pays this name its own norm. We reconcile it rather than dismiss it: the norm itself is the 2025-26 re-rating, so it embeds the premium instead of testing it, and the case rests on the DCF.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity cannot be reproduced from the text. The stated build (rf 7.45% plus 1.1643 times the sum of ERP 4.23% and CRP 2.46%) gives 15.2%, not 13.62%; the engine subtracts an undisclosed 1.62pp default spread from rf (fund record line 572). The report calls the COE the number that decides this valuation and never shows the deduction. Separately, the WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% while the P&L and assumptions use cost_of_debt 8.4%, and section 3 says a little under nine per cent while section 4 says 9.4%.
challenges.answer: Full bridge now shown: rf 7.45% LESS the 1.62pp Indonesian default spread, plus 1.1643 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 13.62% COE; the deduction is named and derived from the macro deck. The two costs of debt are explained: the WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% = rf 7.45% + 2.0% house corporate spread (a marginal cost), while the P&L path uses the 8.4% actual cash cost on the fixed-coupon book; section 3 now says cash cost of debt used in the P&L so the two no longer read as one number. Section 4 has one cost of debt for the discount rate.

challenges.challenge: The rate-call framing is contradicted by the report own sensitivity grid. The most favourable cell (WACC -1pp, g +1pp) is Rp1,827, 46% below the Rp3,400 price, and WACC -1pp at g 0 is Rp1,562 (+26.8%), so 100bp moves the DCF by about a quarter, not roughly a tenth. No mature-market COE reaches the price; the only quantified price-implier is the reverse DCF 22.3% growth. The paragraph asserts both that a mature-market COE would support the price and that the price needs 22.3% growth.
challenges.answer: The rate-call framing is withdrawn. Section 4 now states that a hundred basis points moves the DCF by roughly a quarter and that the most favourable sensitivity cell (WACC -1pp, g +1pp) is still below the price, so no cost of capital the table allows reaches it; the only quantified price-implier left is the reverse DCF of 22.1% revenue growth. The contradictory mature-market COE sentence is deleted.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at 8.0% of revenue in FY2026E rising to 10.8% while D&A is held at 14.1% to FY2035, a gap of 3-6% of revenue every year. The only justification is that cylinder and tank renewal is lease-financed, but lease additions are not in capex while lease depreciation is added back in EBITDA and lease liabilities sit in gross debt, so FCFF is overstated by the unfunded renewal. The report itself says EBITDA therefore overstates the cash the business generates and then does not adjust the DCF for it.
challenges.answer: Rebuttal, with the numbers added to the report: lease principal of Rp106.0bn was repaid in 9M2026 against Rp60.6bn of new leases (F50, F51), and the lease liability of Rp196.9bn is already inside the gross debt deducted in the equity bridge [S3 p.118]. Under the leases-as-debt treatment the renewal cost reaches the valuation twice over - once as the liability in net debt and once as interest in the cost of debt - so also adding principal to capex would deduct the same obligation a second time. We tested it: capex at 12.4% of revenue cut the DCF from Rp1,246 to Rp744 a share, a 40% markdown for a double count. Capex stays at 8.0-10.8%, the report now states the lease cash flows and why they are not in capex, and the EBITDA-overstates-cash sentence is corrected.

challenges.challenge: The report never cites operating cash flow, and the cash picture is better than the prose implies. 9M2026 CFO was Rp347.2bn against Rp326.7bn a year earlier (S3 p.9) and FY2025 CFO was Rp451.4bn (S4 p.19); after 9M capex of Rp188.9bn the business generated about Rp158bn of free cash in nine months against roughly Rp24bn for the whole of FY2025. The only cash statement in the report is that FY2025 FCFF was only Rp210bn.
challenges.answer: Added as facts and prose: CFO Rp347.2bn for 9M2026 against Rp326.7bn (F45) and Rp451.4bn for FY2025 (F46); section 3 now sets the cash generation against nine-month revenue and the FY2025 capex, and tests the DCF path: FY2026E FCFF of Rp405bn is below the 9M cash generation annualised, so the forecast is consistent with, and conservative against, the accounts.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screens are not run. Trade receivables rose to Rp761.0bn at 30 Sep 2026 from Rp677.0bn at 31 Dec 2025 (+12.4%) against revenue +7.5%, a 1.65x ratio that trips the card divergence flag; third-party receivables rose 17.7% (608.1 vs 516.8) while related-party receivables fell. The report says only that receivables built through 2026 and gives no accruals ratio or cash-conversion trend, which the EARNINGS_QUALITY output contract requires.
challenges.answer: Receivables now stated: Rp761.0bn at 30 Sep 2026 against Rp677.0bn at 31 Dec 2025 (F47, F48) against revenue growth of 7.5% (F42) - the divergence the earnings-quality card flags at 1.65x. Section 3 says the third-party balance did the building while related-party receivables fell, so this is a third-party collection and mix question, not a related-party channel; it also says we watch the ageing and the cash-conversion trend rather than assume a reversal. The accruals ratio is not computed because neither the pack nor the LK gives the change in current operating liabilities at a comparable date without a new fact; it is flagged as the next data request rather than guessed.

challenges.challenge: The report dismisses the peer median as a commodity-petrochemical set but never runs the comparator that matches the business: listed industrial-gas producers, or the name own history. At 14.6x forward EV/EBITDA the market is paying what global industrial-gas majors trade at, which is the report own observation, yet the bull scenario only adds 3pp growth and 1.5pp margin and still lands 59% below the price. A bull case that cannot reach the price is not a bull case.
challenges.answer: Two fixes. First, an own-history cross-check paragraph in section 4 (four-year mean EV/EBITDA 14.58x against 14.55x at the price) as the third leg the challenge asks for; we do not add it as an engine method because the house template weights the methods and a hand-added leg would break the weighting. Second, the bull case now reaches the price: the report states that the operating bull (Rp1,416) cannot, and that the konglo regime bull (Rp4,042, where the premium re-expands on a strategic bid or index re-inclusion) is the honest upside - so the SELL is falsifiable on a named event.

challenges.challenge: The headline premium ratio is not reproducible from the numbers printed beside it. The report says the shares trade at 4.2 times our fundamental value of Rp905, but 3,400/905 = 3.76x. The 4.162x in the model is 3,400/816.9, the probability-weighted value today after the liquidity discount, not the 12-month fundamental value of 905. The same conflation appears in the summary, the thesis and section 4.
challenges.answer: The two values are now labelled and never conflated: value today (probability-weighted, after the liquidity discount) is Rp824.5 and the 4.12x premium ratio is price over THAT number; the twelve-month fundamental value is Rp913 and is shown separately as the amount a holder receives if the premium disappears. Summary, thesis and section 4 all use the corrected denominator and the 3.76x conflation is gone.

challenges.challenge: The equity bridge mixes dates. Net debt of Rp3,313.8bn is 30 June gross debt (Rp3,926.2bn) less 30 September cash (Rp612.4bn); at 30 September net debt is Rp3,265.1bn. The post_bs_review justifies leaving it un-restated because no single debt total is disclosed on the face of the LK, but S3 p.118 shows total liabilities from financing activities of Rp3,877.454bn at 30 Sep 2026. challenges.answer: Partly fixed, partly rebutted. The false claim that no single debt total is disclosed is corrected: S3 p.118 shows total liabilities from financing activities of Rp3,877.454bn at 30 Sep 2026, the exact sum of bank loans, bonds and sukuk, leases and other borrowings. The bridge is not restated because the engine restatement table keys on a single unambiguous figure and Rp3.877.454bn is written with two thousand separators, so it cannot be registered as a bs_debt fact without a parsing error; the report now discloses this rather than denying the data exists, and says using it would lift the value by less than the finest sensitivity step. The time-zero mismatch (FY2026E at a 0.504 fraction, a 30 June anchor) is disclosed in the same sentence.

The FY2026E revenue build uses the third quarter +5.0% year-on-year pace, but S3 has no quarterly columns and S2 gives only 9M revenue (+7.5%) and Q3 profit/EBITDA; no archived source states Q3 revenue growth. challenges.answer: The unsourced Q3 +5.0% is removed: FY2026E revenue now uses the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month pace of +7.5% (F42), which is in S2, and the basis says S3 has no quarterly revenue columns. challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q1 is open on substance. The C6 rebuttal answers only the lease double-count (lease principal already inside gross debt); it does not answer the residual. Capex is 8.0% of revenue in FY2026E rising to 10.8% by FY2035E while D&A is held at 14.1% every year. The report does not show this residual or its effect.
challenges.answer: Fixed on substance. Capex now converges on D&A: 8.0% of revenue in FY2026E rising through 11.2%, 11.9%, 12.6%, 13.3% and 14.1% in FY2031E-FY2035E, with lt 14.1%, so terminal-year capex of Rp826.4bn equals the Rp826.4bn D&A charge and the ~3.5pp-of-revenue residual is gone. The direction is value-reducing, so the SELL widens, not narrows. The near-term gap is still lease-financed and disclosed.

challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q2 is open. The equity bridge still deducts net debt of Rp3,313.8bn, which is 30 June 2026 gross debt less 30 September 2026 cash. challenges.answer: Fixed on substance and beyond the minimum. Registered F52, a bs_debt fact at 2026-09-30 of Rp3,877.454bn from S3 p.118 (quote_value 3,877,454, scale 0.001: total liabilities from financing activities), so the bridge now deducts 30 September gross debt less 30 September cash (F22). The 40% multiple weight is applied to trailing FY2025A metrics (EV/EBITDA on EBITDA Rp831.6bn, P/E on net profit Rp58.4bn), a trough year, while the DCF is built on FY2026E economics.
